name: Proof by induction

statementText.CP1.1: Construct proofs using mathematical induction. Contexts include sums of series, divisibility and powers of matrices.

name: Complex numbers: arithmetic, conjugates, roots of polynomials and Argand diagrams

statementText.CP2.1: Solve any quadratic equation with real coefficients. Solve cubic or quartic equations with real coefficients.
statementText.CP2.2: Add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers in the form x + iy with x and y real. Understand and use the terms ‘real part’ and ‘imaginary part’.
statementText.CP2.3: Understand and use the complex conjugate. Know that non-real roots of polynomial equations with real coefficients occur in conjugate pairs.

name: Modulus-argument form

statementText.CP2.5: Convert between the Cartesian form and the modulus-argument form of a complex number.
statementText.CP2.6: Multiply and divide complex numbers in modulus argument form.

name: Loci in the Argand diagram

statementText.CP2.7: Construct and interpret simple loci in the Argand diagram such as |z − a| > r and arg(z − a) = θ.

name: De Moivre's theorem and exponential form

statementText.CP2.8: Understand de Moivre’s theorem and use it to find multiple angle formulae and sums of series.
statementText.CP2.9: Know and use the definition e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ and the form z = re^(iθ).

name: nth roots and roots of unity

statementText.CP2.10: Find the n distinct nth roots of re^(iθ) for r ≠ 0 and know that they form the vertices of a regular n-gon in the Argand diagram.
statementText.CP2.11: Use complex roots of unity to solve geometric problems.

name: Matrices: multiplication, determinants and inverses

statementText.CP3.1: Add, subtract and multiply conformable matrices. Multiply a matrix by a scalar.
statementText.CP3.2: Understand and use zero and identity matrices.
statementText.CP3.5: Calculate determinants of 2 x 2 and 3 x 3 matrices and interpret as scale factors, including the effect on orientation.
statementText.CP3.6: Understand and use singular and non-singular matrices. Properties of inverse matrices. Calculate and use the inverse of non-singular 2 x 2 matrices and 3 x 3 matrices.

name: Linear transformations and invariant points and lines

statementText.CP3.3: Use matrices to represent linear transformations in 2-D. Successive transformations. Single transformations in 3-D.
statementText.CP3.4: Find invariant points and lines for a linear transformation.

name: Three linear equations: solutions and planes

statementText.CP3.7: Solve three linear simultaneous equations in three variables by use of the inverse matrix.
statementText.CP3.8: Interpret geometrically the solution and failure of solution of three simultaneous linear equations.

name: Roots of polynomials

statementText.CP4.1: Understand and use the relationship between roots and coefficients of polynomial equations up to quartic equations.
statementText.CP4.2: Form a polynomial equation whose roots are a linear transformationof the roots of a given polynomial equation (of at least cubic degree).

name: Series: standard sums and the method of differences

statementText.CP4.3: Understand and use formulae for the sums of integers, squares and cubes and use these to sum other series.
statementText.CP4.4: Understand and use the method of differences for summation of series including use of partial fractions.

name: Maclaurin series

statementText.CP4.5: Find the Maclaurin series of a function including the general term.
statementText.CP4.6: Recognise and use the Maclaurin series for eˣ, ln(1 + x), sin x, cos x and (1 + x)ⁿ, and be aware of the range of values of x for which they are valid (proof not required).

name: Volumes of revolution

statementText.CP5.1: Derive formulae for and calculate volumes of revolution.

name: Improper integrals and the mean value of a function

statementText.CP5.2: Evaluate improper integrals where either the integrand is undefined at a value in the range of integration or the range of integration extends to infinity.
statementText.CP5.3: Understand and evaluate the mean value of a function.

name: Integration with partial fractions
Calculus with inverse trigonometric functions

statementText.CP5.6: Integrate functions of the form (a² − x²)^(−1/2) and (a² + x²)^(−1) and be able to choose trigonometric substitutions to integrate associated functions.

name: Vectors: equations of lines and planes, scalar product

statementText.CP6.1: Understand and use the vector and Cartesian forms of an equation of a straight line in 3-D.
statementText.CP6.2: Understand and use the vector and Cartesian forms of the equation of a plane.
statementText.CP6.3: Calculate the scalar product and use it to express the equation of a plane, and to calculate the angle between two lines, the angle between two planes and the angle between a line and a plane.
statementText.CP6.4: Check whether vectors are perpendicular by using the scalar product.

name: Vectors: intersections, angles and shortest distances

statementText.CP6.5: Find the intersection of a line and a plane. Calculate the perpendicular distance between two lines, from a point to a line and from a point to a plane.

name: Polar coordinates: curves and areas

statementText.CP7.1: Understand and use polar coordinates and be able to convert between polar and Cartesian coordinates.
statementText.CP7.2: Sketch curves with r given as a function of θ, including use of trigonometric functions.
statementText.CP7.3: Find the area enclosed by a polar curve.

name: Hyperbolic functions

statementText.CP8.1: Understand the definitions of hyperbolic functions sinh x, cosh x and tanh x, including their domains and ranges, and be able to sketch their graphs.
statementText.CP8.3: Understand and be able to use the definitions of the inverse hyperbolic functions and their domains and ranges.
statementText.CP8.4: Derive and use the logarithmic forms of the inverse hyperbolic functions.
statementText.CP8.5: Integrate functions of the form (x² + a²)^(−1/2) and (x² − a²)^(−1/2) and be able to choose substitutions to integrate associated functions.

name: First-order differential equations: integrating factors and modelling

statementText.CP9.1: Find and use an integrating factor to solve differential equations of form dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) and recognise when it is appropriate to do so.
statementText.CP9.2: Find both general and particular solutions to differential equations.
statementText.CP9.3: Use differential equations in modelling in kinematics and in other contexts.

name: Second-order differential equations

statementText.CP9.4: Solve differential equations of form y″ + ay′ + by = 0 where a and b are constants by using the auxiliary equation.
statementText.CP9.5: Solve differential equations of form y″ + ay′ + by = f(x) where a and b are constants by solving the homogeneous case and adding a particular integral to the complementary function (in cases where f(x) is a polynomial, exponential or trigonometric function).
statementText.CP9.6: Understand and use the relationship between the cases when the discriminant of the auxiliary equation is positive, zero and negative and the form of solution of the differential equation.

name: Simple harmonic motion and damped oscillations

statementText.CP9.7: Solve the equation for simple harmonic motion ẍ = −ω²x and relate the solution to the motion.
statementText.CP9.8: Model damped oscillations using second order differential equations and interpret their solutions.

name: Coupled first-order differential equations

statementText.CP9.9: Analyse and interpret models of situations with one independent variable and two dependent variables as a pair of coupled first order simultaneous equations and be able to solve them, for example predator-prey models.

name: The t-formulae

statementText.FP1.1.2: Applications of t-formulae to trigonometric identities
statementText.FP1.1.3: Applications of t-formulae to solve trigonometric equations

name: Taylor series, limits, Leibnitz's theorem, L'Hospital's rule and the Weierstrass substitution

statementText.FP1.2.1: Derivation and use of Taylor series.
statementText.FP1.2.2: Use of series expansions to find limits.

name: Further differential equations: Taylor series solutions and substitutions

statementText.FP1.3.1: Use of Taylor series method for series solution of differential equations.
statementText.FP1.3.2: Differential equations reducible by means of a given substitution.

name: Conic sections: parabola, ellipse and hyperbola

statementText.FP1.4.1: Cartesian and parametric equations for the parabola and rectangular hyperbola, ellipse and hyperbola.
statementText.FP1.4.2: The focus-directrix properties of the parabola, ellipse and hyperbola, including the eccentricity.
statementText.FP1.4.3: Tangents and normals to these curves.

name: Vector product and scalar triple product

statementText.FP1.5.1: The vector product a × b of two vectors.
statementText.FP1.5.2: The scalar triple product a.b × c
statementText.FP1.5.3: Applications of vectors to three dimensional geometry involving points, lines and planes.

name: Numerical methods: differential equations and Simpson's rule

statementText.FP1.6.1: Numerical solution of first order and second order differential equations.

name: Inequalities

statementText.FP1.7.1: The manipulation and solution of algebraic inequalities and inequations, including those involving the modulus sign.

name: Groups: axioms, Cayley tables, subgroups, Lagrange and isomorphism

statementText.FP2.1.2: Examples of groups. Cayley tables. Cyclic groups.
statementText.FP2.1.3: The order of a group and the order of an element. Subgroups.

name: Reduction formulae, arc length and surface area

statementText.FP2.2.2: The calculation of arc length and the area of a surface of revolution.

name: Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, diagonalisation and Cayley-Hamilton

statementText.FP2.3.1: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 matrices.
statementText.FP2.3.2: Reduction of matrices to diagonal form.
statementText.FP2.3.3: The use of the Cayley-Hamilton theorem.

name: Further complex numbers: regions and transformations of the plane

statementText.FP2.4.1: Further loci and regions in the Argand diagram.
statementText.FP2.4.2: Elementary transformations from the z-plane to the w-plane.

name: Number theory: Euclid, Bezout, modular arithmetic and Fermat

statementText.FP2.5.1: An understanding of the division theorem and its application to the Euclidean Algorithm and congruences.
statementText.FP2.5.3: Modular arithmetic. Understanding what is meant by two integers a and b to be congruent modulo an integer n. Properties of congruences.

name: Combinatorics: counting, permutations and combinations

statementText.FP2.5.7: Combinatorics: counting problems, permutations and combinations.

name: Recurrence relations and proof of closed forms

statementText.FP2.6.1: First and second order recurrence relations.
statementText.FP2.6.2: The solution of recurrence relations to obtain closed forms.
statementText.FP2.6.3: Proof by induction of closed forms.

name: Discrete random variables: mean and variance

statementText.FS1.1.1: Calculation of the mean and variance of discrete probability distributions. Extension of expected value function to include E(g(X))

name: Poisson and binomial distributions

statementText.FS1.2.1: The Poisson distribution The additive property of Poisson distributions
statementText.FS1.2.2: The mean and variance of the binomial distribution and the Poisson distribution.
statementText.FS1.2.3: The use of the Poisson distribution as an approximation to the binomial distribution.

name: Geometric and negative binomial distributions

statementText.FS1.3.2: Mean and variance of a geometric distribution with parameter p.
statementText.FS1.3.3: Mean and variance of negative binomial distribution with P(X = x) = C(x − 1, r − 1) pʳ(1 − p)^(x − r).

name: Hypothesis tests: Poisson, binomial and geometric

statementText.FS1.4.1: Extend ideas of hypothesis tests to test for the mean of a Poisson distribution
statementText.FS1.4.2: Extend hypothesis testing to test for the parameter p of a geometric distribution.

name: Central limit theorem

statementText.FS1.5.1: Applications of the Central Limit Theorem to other distributions.

name: Chi-squared tests: goodness of fit and contingency tables

statementText.FS1.6.1: Goodness of fit tests and Contingency Tables. The null and alternative hypotheses. The use of Σ(Oᵢ − Eᵢ)²/Eᵢ (i = 1 to n) as an approximate χ² statistic. Degrees of freedom.

name: Probability generating functions

statementText.FS1.7.1: Definitions, derivations and applications. Use of the probability generating function for the negative binomial, geometric, binomial and Poisson distributions.
statementText.FS1.7.2: Use to find the mean and variance.
statementText.FS1.7.3: Probability generating function of the sum of independent random variables.

name: Quality of tests: Type I and Type II errors, size and power

statementText.FS1.8.1: Type I and Type II errors. Size and Power of Test. The power function.

name: Linear regression and residuals

statementText.FS2.1.1: Least squares linear regression. The concept of residuals and minimising the sum of squares of residuals.
statementText.FS2.1.2: Residuals. The residual sum of squares (RSS)

name: Continuous random variables and the uniform distribution

statementText.FS2.2.1: The concept of a continuous random variable. The probability density function and the cumulative distribution function for a continuous random variable.
statementText.FS2.2.2: Relationship between probability density and cumulative distribution functions.
statementText.FS2.2.3: Mean and variance of continuous random variables. Extension of expected value function to include E(g(X)) Mode, median and percentiles of continuous random variables. Idea of skewness

name: Correlation: PMCC, Spearman's rank and tests

statementText.FS2.3.1: Use of formulae to calculate the product moment correlation coefficient. Knowledge of the conditions for the use of the product moment correlation coefficient. A knowledge of the effects of coding will be expected.
statementText.FS2.3.2: Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient, its use, interpretation.
statementText.FS2.3.3: Testing the hypothesis that a correlation is zero using either Spearman’s rank correlation or the product moment correlation coefficient.

name: Combinations of random variables

statementText.FS2.4.1: Distribution of linear combinations of independent Normal random variables.

name: Estimators, confidence intervals and tests using the normal distribution

statementText.FS2.5.1: Concepts of standard error, estimator, bias. Quality of estimators
statementText.FS2.5.2: Concept of a confidence interval and its interpretation.
statementText.FS2.5.3: Confidence limits for a Normal mean, with variance known.
statementText.FS2.5.4: Hypothesis test for the difference between the means of two Normal distributions with variances known.
statementText.FS2.5.5: Use of large sample results to extend to the case in which the population variances are unknown.

name: Variance tests: chi-squared and F-distribution

statementText.FS2.6.1: Hypothesis test and confidence interval for the variance of a Normal distribution.
statementText.FS2.6.2: Hypothesis test that two independent random samples are from Normal populations with equal variances.

name: The t-distribution: t-tests and paired t-tests

statementText.FS2.7.1: Hypothesis test and confidence interval for the mean of a Normal distribution with unknown variance.
statementText.FS2.7.3: Hypothesis test and confidence interval for the difference between two means from independent Normal distributions when the variances are equal but unknown. Use of the pooled estimate of variance.

name: Momentum and impulse

statementText.FM1.1.1: Momentum and impulse. The impulse- momentum principle. The principle of conservation of momentum applied to two spheres colliding directly.
statementText.FM1.1.2: Momentum as a vector. The impulse-momentum principle in vector form.

name: Work, energy and power

statementText.FM1.2.1: Kinetic and potential energy, work and power. The work- energy principle. The principle of conservation of mechanical energy.

name: Elastic strings and springs, Hooke's law and elastic energy

statementText.FM1.3.1: Elastic strings and springs. Hooke’s law.
statementText.FM1.3.2: Energy stored in an elastic string or spring.

name: Elastic collisions in one dimension

statementText.FM1.4.1: Direct impact of elastic spheres. Newton’s law of restitution. Loss of kinetic energy due to impact.
statementText.FM1.4.2: Successive direct impacts of spheres and/or a sphere with a smooth plane surface.

name: Elastic collisions in two dimensions (oblique impact)

statementText.FM1.5.1: Oblique impact of smooth elastic spheres and a smooth sphere with a fixed surface. Loss of kinetic energy due to impact.
statementText.FM1.5.2: Successive oblique impacts of a sphere with smooth plane surfaces.

name: Motion in a circle: horizontal and vertical

statementText.FM2.1.1: Angular speed. v = rω. Uniform motion of a particle moving in a horizontal circle. Radial acceleration in circular motion. The forms rω² and v²/r are required.
statementText.FM2.1.2: Motion of a particle in a vertical circle. Radial and tangential acceleration in circular motion. Kinetic and potential energy and the conservation of energy principle applied to motion in a vertical circle.

name: Centres of mass of plane figures

statementText.FM2.2.1: Moment of a force. Centre of mass of a discrete mass distribution in one and two dimensions.
statementText.FM2.2.2: Centre of mass of uniform plane figures, and of composite plane figures. Centre of mass of frameworks. Equilibrium of a plane lamina or framework under the action of coplanar forces.

name: Centres of mass of rigid bodies, equilibrium, toppling and sliding

statementText.FM2.3.1: Centre of mass of uniform and non-uniform rigid bodies and composite bodies.
statementText.FM2.3.2: Equilibrium of rigid bodies under the action of coplanar forces.
statementText.FM2.3.3: Toppling and sliding of a rigid body on a rough plane.

name: Further dynamics: variable forces and simple harmonic motion

statementText.FM2.4.1: Newton’s laws of motion, for a particle moving in one dimension, when the applied force is variable.
statementText.FM2.4.2: Simple harmonic motion. Oscillations of a particle attached to the end of elastic string(s) or spring(s). Kinetic, potential and elastic energy in the context of SHM.

name: Further kinematics: acceleration as a function of time, displacement or velocity

statementText.FM2.5.1: Kinematics of a particle moving in a straight line when the acceleration is a function of the displacement (x), or time (t) or velocity (v).

name: Algorithms, sorting, bin packing and graph theory

statementText.D1.1.1: The general ideas of algorithms and the implementation of an algorithm given by a flow chart or text.
statementText.D1.1.2: Bin packing, bubble sort and quick sort.
statementText.D1.1.3: Use of the order of the nodes to determine whether a graph is Eulerian, semi- Eulerian or neither.
statementText.D1.1.4: The planarity algorithm for planar graphs.

name: Minimum spanning trees (Prim, Kruskal) and shortest paths (Dijkstra, Floyd)

statementText.D1.2.1: The minimum spanning tree (minimum connector) problem. Prim’s and Kruskal’s algorithm.
statementText.D1.2.2: Dijkstra’s and Floyd’s algorithm for finding the shortest path.

name: Route inspection and the travelling salesman problem

statementText.D1.3.1: Algorithm for finding the shortest route around a network, travelling along every edge at least once and ending at the start vertex (The Route Inspection Algorithm).
statementText.D1.3.2: The practical and classical Travelling Salesman problems. The classical problem for complete graphs satisfying the triangle inequality. Determination of upper and lower bounds using minimum spanning tree methods. The nearest neighbour algorithm.

name: Critical path analysis

statementText.D1.4.1: Modelling of a project by an activity network, from a precedence table.
statementText.D1.4.2: Completion of the precedence table for a given activity network.
statementText.D1.4.3: Algorithm for finding the critical path. Earliest and latest event times. Earliest and latest start and finish times for activities. Identification of critical activities and critical path(s).
statementText.D1.4.4: Calculation of the total float of an activity. Construction of Gantt (cascade) charts.
statementText.D1.4.5: Construct resource histograms (including resource levelling) based on the number of workers required to complete each activity.
statementText.D1.4.6: Scheduling the activities using the least number of workers required to complete the project.

name: Linear programming: formulation, graphs and the Simplex algorithm

statementText.D1.5.1: Formulation of problems as linear programs including the meaning and use of slack, surplus and artificial variables.
statementText.D1.5.2: Graphical solution of two variable problems using objective line and vertex methods including cases where integer solutions are required.
statementText.D1.5.3: The Simplex algorithm and tableau for maximising and minimising problems with ≤ constraints.
statementText.D1.5.4: The two-stage Simplex and big-M methods for maximising and minimising problems which may include both ≤ and ≥ constraints.

name: Transportation problems

statementText.D2.1.1: The north-west corner method for finding an initial basic feasible solution.
statementText.D2.1.2: Use of the stepping- stone method for obtaining an improved solution. Improvement indices.
statementText.D2.1.3: Formulation of the transportation problem as a linear programming problem.

name: Allocation (assignment) problems and the Hungarian algorithm

statementText.D2.2.1: Cost matrix reduction. Students should reduce rows first. Use of the Hungarian algorithm to find a least cost allocation. Modification of the Hungarian algorithm to deal with a maximum profit allocation.
statementText.D2.2.2: Formulation of the Hungarian algorithm as a linear programming problem.

name: Flows in networks

statementText.D2.3.2: Use of the labelling procedure to augment a flow to determine the maximum flow in a network.
statementText.D2.3.3: Use of the max–flow min–cut theorem to prove that a flow is a maximum flow.
statementText.D2.3.4: Multiple sources and sinks. Vertices with restricted capacity.
statementText.D2.3.5: Determine the optimal flow rate in a network, subject to given constraints.

name: Dynamic programming

statementText.D2.4.1: Principles of dynamic programming. Bellman’s principle of optimality. Stage variables and State variables. Use of tabulation to solve maximum, minimum, minimax or maximin problems.

name: Game theory

statementText.D2.5.1: Two person zero-sum games and the pay-off matrix.
statementText.D2.5.2: Identification of play safe strategies and stable solutions (saddle points).
statementText.D2.5.3: Reduction of pay-off matrices using dominance arguments.
statementText.D2.5.4: Optimal mixed strategies for a game with no stable solution by use of graphical methods for 2 × n or n × 2 games where n = 1, 2, 3 or 4.
statementText.D2.5.5: Optimal mixed strategies for a game with no stable solution by converting games to linear programming problems that can be solved by the Simplex algorithm.

name: Recurrence relations (Decision 2)

statementText.D2.6.1: Use of recurrence relations to model appropriate problems.
statementText.D2.6.2: Solution of first and second order linear homogeneous and non-homogeneous recurrence relations.

name: Decision analysis: decision trees and expected values

statementText.D2.7.1: Use, construct and interpret decision trees.
statementText.D2.7.2: Use of expected monetary values (EMVs) and utility to compare alternative courses of action.
